title: Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning
authority: Sweller founded cognitive load theory; this is its originating paper.
caveats: Early formulation; later versions of CLT replaced the original load typology (intrinsic/extraneous/germane) and added evolutionary grounding. Criticized as hard to falsify and measure (de Jong 2010). title: Working memory
container: The Psychology of Learning and Motivation, Vol. 8
authority: Baddeley is the leading working memory theorist; this chapter introduced the multicomponent model that underlies modality and dual-channel arguments.
caveats: Model revised (episodic buffer added by Baddeley 2000). The visuospatial/phonological split is well supported; claims that it maps neatly to instructional modality effects are inferential. Bibliographic details (DOI, pages) not confirmed by search this session (search budget exhausted); title, authors, venue and year are from memory.

title: Cognitive load theory and the format of instruction
authority: Original experimental demonstration of the split-attention effect (with Chandler and Sweller 1992 in British Journal of Educational Psychology 62, 233-246, on redundancy and the split-attention effect).
caveats: Early experiments used technical material and small samples; effect depends on diagram and text being unintelligible alone. Later meta-analysis (Ginns 2006) supports spatial contiguity effect but with moderators. Bibliographic details (DOI, pages) not confirmed by search this session (search budget exhausted); title, authors, venue and year are from memory.

title: Cognitive architecture and instructional design
authority: Comprehensive review of cognitive load theory by its principal authors; among the most cited papers in the field. Updated by the same authors in 2019 (Educational Psychology Review 31(2), 261-292).
caveats: Author-group review, not independent. Load measurement (subjective ratings, dual-task) remains contested.

title: Multimedia Learning
authority: Mayer is the leading researcher on multimedia learning; this book states the cognitive theory of multimedia learning (CTML) and the principles.
caveats: Most experiments use short lab lessons (lightning, pumps, brakes) with immediate tests and novice college students; effect sizes are medians across the author's own lab work and may overstate effects in long-term real-world use. Some principles have boundary conditions. Bibliographic details (DOI, pages) not confirmed by search this session (search budget exhausted); title, authors, venue and year are from memory. Effect-size medians quoted in notes are not confirmed.

title: Nine ways to reduce cognitive load in multimedia learning
authority: Mayer and Moreno are authors of the CTML/CATLM frameworks; this paper maps overload scenarios to design remedies.
caveats: Principle list has since been expanded and reorganized; effects mostly shown with novices in short lessons.

title: The expertise reversal effect
authority: Key CLT paper showing that design techniques that help novices can hurt experts; foundational for adaptive instruction.
caveats: Reversal is graded, not sharp; depends on accurate expertise diagnosis. Kalyuga's 2007 review extends it.

title: Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work: An analysis of the failure of constructivist, discovery, problem-based, experiential, and inquiry-based teaching
authority: Highly cited position paper by leading CLT researchers; central to the guided-instruction argument.
caveats: Contested: Hmelo-Silver, Duncan and Chinn (2007) and Schmidt et al. (2007) argued that problem-based and inquiry learning are scaffolded, not minimal guidance. Kirschner et al. mostly address novices (expertise reversal applies). Bibliographic details (DOI, pages) not confirmed by search this session (search budget exhausted); title, authors, venue and year are from memory.

title: How seductive details do their damage: A theory of cognitive interest in science learning
authority: Experimental test of why interesting but irrelevant material harms learning (diversion, disruption and priming accounts).
caveats: Lab studies with short passages (lightning); later work shows effect varies by seduction type and learner characteristics. Bibliographic details (DOI, pages) not confirmed by search this session (search budget exhausted); title, authors, venue and year are from memory.

title: A review of research and a meta-analysis of the seductive detail effect
authority: First meta-analysis of seductive details (39 effects); reports small-to-medium retention and medium transfer harm.
caveats: Heterogeneous studies; later meta-analysis (Sundararajan and Adesope 2020, Educational Psychology Review) refines it and finds moderators; effect depends on type (text vs. pictures) and learner prior knowledge.

title: Animation: Can it facilitate?
authority: Influential review arguing animation advantages are usually confounded with extra information or interactivity (apprehension and congruence principles).
caveats: Review from 2002; later meta-analyses show a small animation advantage for dynamic content. Principles are conceptual rather than quantified.

title: Instructional animation versus static pictures: A meta-analysis
authority: Meta-analysis of 26 studies and 76 comparisons; the standard quantitative reference on animation versus static pictures.
caveats: Overall effect cited as d = 0.37 in later reviews (not confirmed against the paper); advantage larger for representational (realistic) than decorative animation; Berney and Bétrancourt (2016) update found a smaller effect (g about 0.23).

title: Emotional design in multimedia learning
authority: Experimental demonstration that warm colors and round, face-like shapes induce positive emotion and improve comprehension and transfer.
caveats: Small student samples; later replications are mixed (Brom et al. 2018 meta-analysis finds small positive effects, with heterogeneity; some failed replications). Bibliographic details (DOI, pages) not confirmed by search this session (search budget exhausted); title, authors, venue and year are from memory.

title: How effective is emotional design? A meta-analysis on facial anthropomorphisms and pleasant colors during multimedia learning
authority: Meta-analysis of 33 samples (N = 2924) of emotional design; most direct test of the claim.
caveats: Narrow operationalization (faces and colors); heterogeneity and possible publication bias; follow-up by Wong and Adesope (2021).

title: A meta-analysis of how signaling affects learning with media
authority: Meta-analysis (reported 103 studies) establishing a reliable but moderate signaling effect.
caveats: Pooled effect sizes not confirmed against the paper; a secondary report cites g about 0.5 (retention) and 0.3 (transfer) and about 103 studies. Effect is smaller with higher prior knowledge and when many cues are used.

title: Why a diagram is (sometimes) worth ten thousand words
authority: Classic computational-cognition analysis from Carnegie Mellon (Simon: Nobel laureate) of when diagrams beat sentences.
caveats: Computational model, not human experiment; claims hold for well-structured diagrams, not any picture.

title: DeFT: A conceptual framework for considering learning with multiple representations
authority: Leading framework for multiple external representations (design, functions, tasks).
caveats: Conceptual framework; empirical support is patchy and domain-specific.

title: Cognitive load theory, educational research, and instructional design: Some food for thought
authority: Principal scholarly critique of cognitive load theory by a respected learning-sciences researcher.
caveats: A critique itself; Sweller and colleagues have replied. Valuable for conceptual (non-falsifiable, measurement) limits. Bibliographic details (DOI, pages) not confirmed by search this session (search budget exhausted); title, authors, venue and year are from memory.
